chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: BIRTH OF THE CONSTITUTION This book tells how a group of unusu- ally talented men joined in 1787 to create a constitution for a new United States and what the Consti- tution has meant over the years.
text_raw:
BIRTH 
OF THE 
CONSTITUTION 
This book tells how a group of unusu- 
ally talented men joined in 1787 
to create a constitution for a new 
United States and what the Consti- 
tution has meant over the years.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The book begins with the events leading up to the Constitutional Convention : the Newburgh Conspiracy (when Continental officers proposed taking over the government), how the colonies were governed after the end of the Revolutionary War, and the proposal that a meeting be held to revise the Articles of Confederation, which was then governing the colonies.
text_raw:
The book begins with the events 
leading up to the Constitutional 
Convention : the Newburgh Conspiracy 
(when Continental officers proposed 
taking over the government), how 
the colonies were governed after the 
end of the Revolutionary War, and 
the proposal that a meeting be held 
to revise the Articles of Confederation, 
which was then governing the colonies.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The second part describes the Constitutional Convention itself: the character of the men who came to the Convention, how the big states wanted one plan and the small ones another, and how compromises paved the way to a solution.
text_raw:
The second part describes the 
Constitutional Convention itself: the 
character of the men who came to 
the Convention, how the big states 
wanted one plan and the small ones 
another, and how compromises paved 
the way to a solution.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The third part tells how the Constitution was created as a living document: how a system of checks and balances was created among the legislative, executive, and judicial branches, how the Bill of Rights was added, how the Supreme Court has interpreted the Constitution, and how the Constitution has been changed by later Amendments.
text_raw:
The third part tells how the 
Constitution was created as a living 
document: how a system of checks 
and balances was created among the 
legislative, executive, and judicial 
branches, how the Bill of Rights 
was added, how the Supreme Court 
has interpreted the Constitution, and 
how the Constitution has been changed 
by later Amendments.

More than sixteen 
months had passed since Lord Cornwallis had surrendered at

text: His band, according to legend, had played "The World Turned Upside Down" to mark the end of Great Brit- ain's control over its American colonies.

text: British troops still occupied New York City, but all the fighting had ceased.

British troops still

chapter_title: Chapter 12 Changing the Constitution in the
text: The draft of a peace treaty had been signed at Paris, and it was now on its way to the American Congress at Philadelphia.
text_raw:
The 
draft of a peace treaty had been signed at Paris, and it was

chapter_title: Chapter 12 Changing the Constitution in the
text: It had been eight long years since those few brave farmers at Lexington and Concord had started the American Revolu- tion by firing "the shots heard round the world." Eight long years of suffering and sacrifice, of going without enough food and warm clothing for weeks on end, of feeling pain and fac- ing death on battlefields turned crimson with young men's blood.

It had been eight long years since those few brave farmers 
at Lexington and Concord had started the American Revolu-

and warm clothing for weeks on end, of feeling pain and fac-

text: But those dark days of agony finally had ended.

text: The kill- ing had stopped.

The kill- 
ing had stopped.

chapter_title: Chapter 12 Changing the Constitution in the
text: And Americans were free at last!
text_raw: And Americans were free at last!

chapter_title: Chapter 12 Changing the Constitution in the
text: Free to shape their own future, free to forge their own nation.
text_raw:
Free to 
shape their own future, free to forge their own nation.

text: More- over, Americans were soon to gain from Britain much more land than they dreamed they would own.
text_raw:
More- 
over, Americans were soon to gain from Britain much more 
land than they dreamed they would own.

text: No longer would they be confined to a narrow strip of land hugging the Atlan- tic coast.

they be confined to a narrow strip of land hugging the Atlan-

text_raw:

text: Americans at that time were governed under a docu- ment known as the Articles of Confederation, and the ruling body was called the Confederation Congress.
text_raw:
Americans at that time were governed under a docu- 
ment known as the Articles of Confederation, and the ruling 
body was called the Confederation Congress.

chapter_title: Chapter 12 Changing the Constitution in the
text: Some of the Americans who had fought in the Revolution- ary War, however, were not as happy as the congressmen in Philadelphia.
text_raw:
Some of the Americans who had fought in the Revolution- 
ary War, however, were not as happy as the congressmen in

chapter_title: Chapter 12 Changing the Constitution in the
text: One group of disgruntled army officers was sta- tioned at Newburgh, New York, in a camp nestled above the Hudson River.
text_raw:
One group of disgruntled army officers was sta- 
tioned at Newburgh, New York, in a camp nestled above the 
Hudson River.

chapter_title: Chapter 12 Changing the Constitution in the
text: General George Washington was at this camp, and he was concerned because some of his most trusted and capable officers were seething with anger.
text_raw:
General George Washington was at this camp, 
and he was concerned because some of his most trusted and 
capable officers were seething with anger.

chapter_title: Chapter 12 Changing the Constitution in the
text: In January 1783 they had sent a committee to Philadelphia to demand some money from the Confederation Congress.
text_raw:
In January 1783 they had sent a committee to Philadelphia 
to demand some money from the Confederation Congress.

chapter_title: Chapter 12 Changing the Constitution in the
text: The committee claimed that the officers had not been paid their wages for months, that their food and clothing allow- ances were long overdue, and that they had been promised a pension but no plans had yet been made to set up this fund.
text_raw:
The committee claimed that the officers had not been paid 
their wages for months, that their food and clothing allow- 
ances were long overdue, and that they had been promised a 
pension but no plans had yet been made to set up this fund.

chapter_title: Chapter 12 Changing the Constitution in the
text: The members of Congress listened sympathetically to the committee's pleas, but they replied that there was not enough money in the treasury to meet any of the officers' demands.
text_raw:
The members of Congress listened sympathetically to the 
committee's pleas, but they replied that there was not enough 
money in the treasury to meet any of the officers' demands.

chapter_title: Chapter 12 Changing the Constitution in the
text: Moreover, Congress had no power to tax the people or the states, so its sources of funds were few and very unreliable.
text_raw:
Moreover, Congress had no power to tax the people or the 
states, so its sources of funds were few and very unreliable.

chapter_title: Chapter 12 Changing the Constitution in the
text: Discouraged and resentful, the committee sent word back to Newburgh that its cause seemed hopeless.
text_raw:
Discouraged and resentful, the committee sent word back to 
Newburgh that its cause seemed hopeless.

chapter_title: Chapter 12 Changing the Constitution in the
text: On March 10, 1783, two unsigned messages were quietly circulated among the officers at Newburgh.
text_raw:
On March 10, 1783, two unsigned messages were quietly 
circulated among the officers at Newburgh.

chapter_title: Chapter 12 Changing the Constitution in the
text: One of them pro- posed that unless Congress could be forced to grant their re- quests, the officers would refuse to disband, "retire to some unsettled country," and leave Congress without an army.

posed that unless Congress could be forced to grant their re-

text: This suggestion infuri- ated Washington, who wrote in his reply to Nicola, "Be as- sured, sir, no occurrence in the course of the war has given me more [unpleasant] sensations." Then he scolded the colo- nel severely.

a majority of the whole number of Electors appointed; and if 
no person have such majority, then from the persons having 
the highest numbers not exceeding three on the list of those 
voted for as President, the House of Representatives shall 
choose immediately, by ballot, the President.

text_raw:
The Congress, 
whenever two-thirds of both houses shall deem it necessary, shall 
propose amendments to this Constitution, or, on the application of 
the legislatures of two-thirds of the several States, shall call a con- 
vention for proposing amendments, which, in either case, shall be 
valid to all intents and purposes, as part of this Constitution, when 
ratified by the legislatures of three-fourths of the several States, or 
by conventions in three-fourths thereof, as the one or the other 
mode of ratification may be proposed by the Congress; provided
